text: Five quick ones to finish, most of them about one model shared by many teams. A conformed dimension is one dimension that several fact tables share, with the same keys and the same values. Sales and inventory both use one date dimension, so you can drill across them and the days line up. A wide table puts one entity on each row, with every attribute a column: fast, and easy in a dashboard, but each new attribute is a new column. A narrow table keeps few columns and joins to the rest: flexible, at the cost of joins. Columnar warehouses handle wide tables well. A bus matrix is a plan: business processes down the side, conformed dimensions across the top, and a tick where a process uses one. A data mart is what gets built: the slice of the warehouse for one domain, like sales. The shared dimensions let two marts be combined. Why a date dimension, rather than date functions? Fiscal quarters and holidays are business rules. Store them once, in a table, and every query just filters and groups. On the page's orders, revenue by fiscal quarter without holidays is one join and no date math. A measure is a raw column on a fact table, like revenue. A metric is a business definition built from measures, like average order value: revenue over orders. Define each metric once, in one shared place. On the page's orders, it's a hundred eighty-six dollars with holidays and a hundred sixty-three without, and two teams could each report one. Every answer here treated a dimension as fixed. But customers move and products get renamed, so the model has to keep history. Next: modeling history.
